questions.stem: The 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were adopted by the United Nations in the year:
questions.explanation: The SDGs / Agenda 2030 were adopted on 25 September 2015 at a UN summit in New York, to replace the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs, 2000-15). 17 Goals + 169 targets + ~230 indicators, covering poverty, hunger, health, education, gender, water, energy, cities, climate etc. NITI Aayog tracks India's SDG progress through the SDG India Index (first released 2018).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The term 'sustainable development' was made famous in 1987 by a report chaired by:

options.option_text: Mahatma Gandhi
Gro Harlem Brundtland
Kofi Annan
Rachel Carson

questions.explanation: The Brundtland Report ('Our Common Future', 1987) by the World Commission on Environment and Development — chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland (former PM of Norway) — defined sustainable development as 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'. Rachel Carson — 'Silent Spring' (1962), DDT-warning book. Kofi Annan — UN Secretary-General (1997-2006).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The target year for the Sustainable Development Goals is:
questions.explanation: SDGs are also called 'Agenda 2030' because of the 2030 target year. The halfway point (2022-23) saw UN reports warning that progress was off-track on most goals after COVID-19, Ukraine war, inflation. India has committed to LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) as a complementary voluntary framework announced by PM Modi at COP-26 (2021).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Goal 13 of the Sustainable Development Goals focuses on:

options.option_text: Gender equality
Climate action
Clean water and sanitation
Affordable and clean energy

questions.explanation: Goal 13 — 'Climate Action' — aims to take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts. Related goals — 7 (affordable clean energy), 6 (water and sanitation), 14 (life below water), 15 (life on land), 11 (sustainable cities), 12 (responsible consumption). Goal 5 is gender equality. Understanding which number maps to which goal is an exam-frequent drill.
questions.subject: Environment

options.option_text: Buying more and discarding quickly
Reduce, reuse, recycle — keeping resources in the loop
Replacing all fossil fuels with wind energy
Moving all industrial activity to rural areas

questions.explanation: Circular economy — reduce resource use, reuse products, recycle materials, so outputs become inputs instead of waste. Opposite of the 'linear' take-make-dispose model. Indian policy examples — plastic waste management rules with EPR, battery swapping, e-waste collection, Fly-ash utilisation. Ellen MacArthur Foundation is a leading global champion. The 3 Rs are increasingly supplemented by 'repair' and 'refuse'.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) — a movement championed by India at COP-26 — emphasises:

options.option_text: Mandatory electric-vehicle use
Mindful, low-waste consumption by individuals
Forest conservation laws
International trade agreements

questions.explanation: Mission LiFE — announced by PM Modi at COP-26 (Glasgow 2021), formally launched 2022 — asks each individual to adopt climate-friendly behaviours (save water, save energy, reduce food waste, avoid single-use plastic, prefer sustainable food, say no to e-waste) rather than expecting change only from governments or industry. The idea is individual agency as a climate lever. UNDP officially backed it in 2022.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) had how many goals?
questions.explanation: MDGs, 2000-15 — eight goals: eradicate extreme poverty/hunger; universal primary education; gender equality; reduce child mortality; maternal health; combat HIV-AIDS, malaria; environmental sustainability; global partnership. Succeeded by the 17 SDGs (2015-30). MDGs were narrower and targeted mainly developing countries; SDGs cover all countries and are broader (cover economic, social, environmental dimensions explicitly).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Which SDG number is assigned to the goal titled 'Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure'?

options.option_text: SDG 7, which covers Affordable and Clean Energy access
SDG 9, which covers Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure
SDG 8, which covers Decent Work and Economic Growth goals
SDG 11, covering Sustainable Cities and Communities goals

questions.explanation: SDG 9 is 'Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure'. The most common confusion is with SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), which sounds similarly economic in scope but focuses on employment and GDP growth, not physical infrastructure and innovation ecosystems.

questions.stem: The three traditional pillars of sustainable development — which underpin the entire SDG framework — are:

options.option_text: Social, Economic, and Environmental sustainability of growth
Political, Cultural, and Technological advancement agendas
Fiscal, Monetary, and Trade policy coordination mechanisms
Health, Education, and Infrastructure development priorities

questions.explanation: Sustainable development rests on three mutually reinforcing pillars: Social (equity/inclusion), Economic (growth/prosperity), and Environmental (ecological integrity). Options B, C, and D conflate specific policy instruments or sectoral goals with the foundational conceptual pillars established at Rio 1992.

questions.stem: The 'planetary boundaries' framework — defining nine safe operating limits for Earth's biophysical systems — was primarily developed by:

options.option_text: James Hansen and colleagues at NASA Goddard Institute, New York
Johan Rockström and colleagues at the Stockholm Resilience Centre
Paul Ehrlich and colleagues at Stanford University, California
Rajendra Pachauri and team at the IPCC Secretariat, Geneva

questions.explanation: Johan Rockström et al. published the planetary boundaries framework in Nature (2009), identifying nine Earth-system processes (climate change, biodiversity loss, ozone depletion, etc.) with quantified safe limits. James Hansen is known for climate modelling, Paul Ehrlich for the population-ecology 'population bomb' thesis, and Pachauri led the IPCC but was not associated with this framework.

questions.stem: Under SDG 12 ('Responsible Consumption and Production'), 'absolute decoupling' specifically means:

options.option_text: Reducing total resource use even as the economy grows in absolute terms
Slowing resource use growth at a pace slower than the GDP growth rate
Shifting production entirely from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources
Eliminating all packaging materials from industrial manufacturing chains

questions.explanation: Absolute decoupling occurs when total resource consumption falls even while GDP rises — the gold standard of SDG 12. Option B describes 'relative decoupling' (resource intensity per unit of GDP falls, but total use still rises), which is a critically different and weaker outcome frequently confused with the absolute form in exam contexts.

questions.stem: Countries present 'Voluntary National Reviews' (VNRs) tracking their SDG progress at which intergovernmental body?

options.option_text: UN General Assembly's Second Committee on economic affairs
High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development (HLPF)
UN Environment Assembly convened biennially at Nairobi, Kenya
UN Commission on Sustainable Development, the pre-2013 body

questions.explanation: VNRs are the flagship accountability mechanism of the SDG era and are presented at the HLPF, which meets annually under ECOSOC and every four years at Heads-of-State level as the SDG Summit. The UN Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD) was the predecessor body but was formally replaced by the HLPF in 2013, making Option D a particularly well-designed distractor.

questions.stem: The 'Environmental Kuznets Curve' (EKC) — widely cited in sustainable-development economics — predicts which relationship between per-capita income and environmental degradation?

options.option_text: Environmental degradation rises steadily and linearly with every GDP increase
Pollution peaks at middle-income levels, then declines as economies advance further
High-income nations systematically export pollution to lower-income countries
Environmental quality improves at low incomes but worsens only at high incomes

questions.explanation: The EKC posits an inverted-U relationship: pollution worsens during early industrialisation, peaks around middle income (as structural shifts to services occur and demand for environmental regulation strengthens), then declines. Option C describes the separate 'Pollution Haven Hypothesis'. Option D inverts the curve incorrectly. The EKC is empirically contested but is a standard concept in SDG policy and environment economics papers.

questions.stem: The principle of 'Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities' (CBDR-RC) was first formally enshrined in which international instrument?

options.option_text: Kyoto Protocol, 1997 — the first legally binding emissions treaty
Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, Principle 7 (1992)
Brundtland Report 'Our Common Future', published by WCED in 1987
Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment, adopted in 1972

questions.explanation: CBDR-RC was first formally codified in Principle 7 of the Rio Declaration (1992). While the Kyoto Protocol (1997) is the first binding treaty to operationalise CBDR-RC through the Annex I/Non-Annex I country differentiation, the principle's original enshrinement was at Rio — not Kyoto, which is the most common mistake. The Brundtland Report (1987) introduced 'sustainable development' conceptually but did not articulate CBDR-RC; Stockholm (1972) predates the principle entirely.
